h: Wandle Walks, Morris Prints and Wimbledon Tennis
p: The River Wandle has a fascinating backstory, and it ties in nicely with a visit to Deen City Farm. Once one of the hardest-working rivers in England, it powered dozens of mills along its banks, producing everything from snuff and flour to printed textiles. The Wandle Trail now follows the river for miles through South London, and it makes a lovely stroll or bike ride to stretch your legs after time with the animals.

One of the river's most famous residents was William Morris, the Victorian designer whose patterns still decorate wallpaper, fabrics and gift shop mugs across the land. In 1881 he set up his workshops at Merton Abbey, using the Wandle's water to print and dye his textiles. Liberty, the London department store, also had print works on the same stretch. Look out for the information boards along the river as you go; older children who enjoy art often find the link to well-known patterns surprisingly exciting.

At the farm, a little planning helps. If anyone fancies a riding lesson, book well in advance rather than hoping for a space on the day. Families with a buggy might find the riverside paths easier than busier pavements, and the café makes a handy meeting point if your group splits up.

Getting around is easy, with Colliers Wood on the Northern line and trams on the Tramlink network nearby. Wimbledon is also close, so tennis fans can add the Wimbledon Lawn Tennis Museum at the All England Club to the day, with its displays of racquets, trophies and famous match moments.
